audience: undergraduate computer science; spoken explanation of 1-3 minutes

key_points.text: Normalisation organises the columns and tables of a relational database to reduce redundant (duplicated) data.
key_points.partial_if: says it 'organises' or 'cleans' the data without mentioning redundancy or duplication

key_points.text: Redundancy causes update, insertion and deletion anomalies (e.g. changing a fact in one row but not another), and normalisation prevents them.
key_points.partial_if: says data can become inconsistent but names no anomaly or example

key_points.text: Tables are decomposed into smaller related tables linked by primary and foreign keys, without losing information (the original data can be rebuilt with joins).
key_points.partial_if: says tables are split but does not mention keys or that nothing is lost

key_points.text: Normal forms are successive levels based on functional dependencies; at least one is described correctly (1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups; 2NF: no partial dependency on part of a composite key; 3NF: no transitive dependency between non-key attributes).
key_points.partial_if: names normal forms (1NF/2NF/3NF) but does not describe what any of them requires, or describes one only loosely

key_points.text: Trade-off: a highly normalised design needs more joins, which can slow some reads, so designs are sometimes deliberately denormalised for performance.
key_points.partial_if: mentions that there is a cost but not what it is

misconceptions.text: The main purpose of normalisation is to make queries run faster.
Database normalisation means scaling numeric values into a fixed range such as 0 to 1 (confusing it with data or feature normalisation).
A database should always be normalised to the highest normal form possible.
